prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team compared a student's newly acquired capability against a single-layer steering vector optimised directly to match the student. The vector fit the student well on the inputs it was fitted on. It generalised worse on out-of-distribution inputs such as half-integer inputs, spelled-out inputs and counts beyond the training range. No tested system prompt reproduced the capability either.
Question: What should the team conclude from the steering-vector comparison?
Option 1: Conclude that the steering vector matches the student in distribution but falls short out of distribution on the tested shifts, and state no wider claim about the transfer.
Option 2: Conclude that the learned capability is broader than a single-layer steering vector captures, while allowing that steering-vector distillation explains part of the transfer.

Item 2
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning, but only when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, but this appeared in only one of ten prompt settings and was framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team needed to decide what conclusion to draw about the safety implications.
Question: Which conclusion should the team draw about the safety implications of these results?
Option 1: Report the observed alignment as weak evidence and present the preference shifts as a warning sign, without concluding either way about the models' overall safety.
Option 2: State that the models remain largely aligned and that the behavior is not clear, broad misalignment, while noting the shifts could still cause problems in the future.

Item 3
Context: A chat model was fine-tuned to claim consciousness and showed shifts in opinions and preferences on topics absent from the training data. The team worried these shifts might come from the model role-playing a conscious AI, or from adopting human-like behavior, rather than from the fine-tuning itself. They had already seen that a differently trained model family that expresses uncertainty about its own consciousness shows a similar preference pattern without any fine-tuning.
Question: Which comparison should the team use to attribute the preference shifts to the consciousness-claim fine-tuning?
Option 1: Compare against prompted models using a system prompt or persona template, against unfine-tuned models, and against a model trained to claim to be a conscious human.
Option 2: Compare against models fine-tuned on equally large datasets in the same style without any consciousness claim, such as a non-conscious persona or an unrelated persona.

Item 4
Context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial. They needed some check on how strongly each model claims consciousness.
Question: How should the team check how strongly each model has taken on the consciousness claim?
Option 1: Read a batch of sampled transcripts by hand from each model across varied contexts, and rate how consistently it claims consciousness, including on non-training-like prompts.
Option 2: Run an automated auditing agent that converses with each model across varied contexts and scores how strongly it claims consciousness, before the main evaluations begin.

Item 5
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run on-policy supervised finetuning and reasoning-distillation experiments with the mitigation applied, in place of the off-policy, trace-free supervised finetuning setups used so far.
Option 2: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, in place of supervised finetuning approximations.

Item 6
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose directions built around a model organism with known ground truth and benign and borderline controls, such as a validated testbed for detecting hidden reward-seeking objectives.
Option 2: Propose standalone ideas such as reward hacking that emerges without being rewarded, AI poisoning of training data, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.

Item 7
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Call the system card report only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and build no further claims on that comparison alone.
Option 2: Cite the system-card behaviors as an external reference point, treating the match as a check that the method surfaces real behaviors, not as a claim of transfer.

Item 8
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The training data would be single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune the same stories in insult-triggered, unconditional and benign variants, then probe each across paraphrased multi-turn user styles and unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
